newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sandvik sees no economic upturn in H1 '97.
newsitem.headline: Sandvik sees no economic upturn in H1 '97.

text.p: Swedish engineer Sandvik AB on Monday posted a larger than expected fall in 1996 profits, saying it saw no large upturn in industrial economic trends in the first half of 1997.
Sandvik said it expected 1997 profits to be about the same level of 1996 when it posted a 21 percent drop in profit after financial items to 4.45 billion crowns.
"No major upturn in the industrial climate is foreseen during the first half of the year," Sandvik said in a statement.
"A nearly unchanged level of earnings is projected for full-year 1997 compared with 1996."
A Reuter poll of 13 analysts found expectations of a profit after financial items of 4.65 billion crowns for 1996, a fall of 17 percent compared with the actual drop of 21 percent.
Despite the lower profit, Sandvik proposed to raise the dividend to 6.50 crowns a share from 6.00 crowns.
"The positive development of Sandvik's earnings and cash flow in recent years has created some over-capitalisation," the company said in a statement.

"In view of this a decision has previously been taken on a revised dividend policy implying a significant increase in dividends. In addition, Sandvik has the ambition to increase its growth rate. "This is expected to gradually reduce the equity ratio."
For 1996, Sandvik's equity to assets ratio was unchanged at 64 percent.
Sandvik's board is also considering proposing to the annual general shareholders' meeting a share redemption worth about four billion crowns, the company said.
"Sandvik has, for some time, awaited legislation allowing share buy backs," the company said.

"Since there is still uncertainty regarding this legislation, the board has decided to investigate alternative measures to improve capital structure, such as reduction of the share capital through a redemption of shares."
The board will present a detailed proposal around two weeks ahead of the annual general meeting on May 6, the company said.
In 1996, order intake fell by eight percent to 27.54 billion crowns, but at fixed foreign exchange rates the decrease was two percent, Sandvik said.

Sales fell five percent to 28.27 billion crowns, mainly because of negative effects from the stronger Swedish crown, which caused Sandvik's invoicing to be seven percent lower in 1996 than what it would have been at 1995 exchange rates.
Total invoiced sales were unchanged between 1996 and 1995, Sandvik said.
"Altogether, Sandvik was able to defend or strengthen its market position and increase market shares even in countries with stagnating or weakening demand," the company said.
